title: CLO 2024 Course: Exploring the New Features of Knitwear Together
description:
CLO2024 Online Live Teaching Begins!  
Join CLO technical expert Celia to explore the versatile applications of the new knitting features in CLO2024.0! Start your creative journey in knitwear design!  
For free materials for this session, please visit the WeChat official account “CLO3D” and reply with “免费素材” (free materials) to receive them.  

Previous courses are available at: https://space.bilibili.com/477753185/channel/collectiondetail?sid=1370949
transcript:
Welcome everyone to the Kele live broadcast room, welcome everyone to the Kele live broadcast room. I am your host for this session, Celia. Welcome everyone to the Kele live broadcast room, I am your host, Celia.

Today’s live broadcast focuses on the new knitwear feature in Kele 2024.0, where we will create some garment styles. Today’s live broadcast focuses on the new knitwear feature in Kele 2024.0, where we will create some garment styles.

First, we will make a basic sweater like this to give everyone a comprehensive understanding of the new knitwear function. Then we will proceed to make a modified design of this style.

You can get the live broadcast materials by scanning the public account QR code at the bottom left corner of the screen, then reply with “free materials” to receive them.

Let’s first open the first basic sweater from the live broadcast materials.

This is a white model that has already been made. Previously, if we wanted to make a sweater, we needed to rely on fabric texture maps, displacement maps, and replacement maps to represent it.

In the new version, we can select the fabric. Then, under the material type below, there is a new option for Knitwear. Click to switch.

You can see in the 3D window that the garment surface now looks like a knitted fabric made by needles.

At the same time, in the property editor, under Knitwear, there are some new options.

Let’s look at them together. First is the stitch type. Currently, this is a suspend needle. Then there is the plain stitch.

Then the reverse stitch.

Single osmanthus stitch. Osmanthus stitch.

And ribbing.

You can take note of these for easy selection of different stitch types later.

There’s also half-rib stitch and honeycomb stitch.

Here, I chose the plain stitch for this sweater.

Below that is knitting density. When adjusted, the smaller the density, the sparser the knitting; the larger the density, the tighter the knitting.

Below is the wales count. The wales count refers to the number of knitting wales per wale unit.

You can switch this between 1 and 6.

For example, if the wales count is 4, you can set the color for each of the four wales below.

You can also modify the colors after changing the wales count. Here, we change it back to white.

Further down is the thickness of the wales. The smaller the value, the thinner the wales; the larger the value, the thicker the wales.

Next, there is an option to generate seams. This option is enabled by default.

We can understand this as automatically creating outward-extending wales at the seam positions of our pattern pieces.

This achieves a natural transition and connection of the garment at the seams.

Here, I turned off the generate seams option. You can see the sleeve seam connection is now broken.

Then turn it back on.

Below is seam bending length and seam bending rate. Seam bending length refers to how far the wales extend outward at the seam.

Currently set to 1, we change it to 0. You can see the seam connection breaks at 0.

Then increase it.

The longer the bending length, the farther the pattern piece extends outward.

Seam bending rate refers to how much the pattern piece curls inward at the seam and edge positions. The smaller the value, the more it curls inward.

The curl is more pronounced.

The larger the value, the flatter the pattern piece.

Next is the valley line normal map.

We can zoom in to see it. On the valley line, there is a bump texture.

If we delete it, the shadowing effect will disappear or weaken.

Ctrl-Z to undo.

Now we can change the collar, cuffs, and hem of the sweater to ribbing fabric.

We can copy the main garment’s fabric first.

Then switch the stitch type to ribbing 2×2.

After switching the fabric, you can see the collar should realistically gradually shrink upward and have a bind-off effect at the edges.

Here, we can select the collar pattern piece in the 3D window.

Then reduce its horizontal scale to about 80%.

Before simulating, we recommend you uncheck the “Display Knitwear” option under render options in the 3D window to speed up simulation.

The hem and cuffs can be operated the same way.

Next, we will handle the bind-off details.

We use the Edit Pattern Piece tool.

Select the outer lines of the collar, hem, and cuffs.

Set an internal line spacing of 2mm.

Right-click on this line.

Choose Cut and Sew.

After modifying the style, you can turn the “Display Knitwear” option back on.

Here, we copy the ribbed fabric again.

Change its stitch type to reverse stitch.

Apply this new fabric to the small pattern pieces we just cut.

Place it on this surface.

Adjust the color of the collar fabric accordingly.

You can see the surface now has a very realistic knitting effect.

Our stitch pattern is done.

Next, we can change the color of the garment.

One way is to set the number of wales mentioned earlier and then set the color of each wale line.

Another way is below.

There is a basic parameter and texture below.

We can add a texture to the sweater.

You can also modify the overall color.

Here, we add a gradient pattern.

In our material file folder, find this pattern, drag it onto our texture.

Change the original color of the five lines to white.

Then use the adjustment texture tool to enlarge the texture and keep only one ring of the pattern.

After modifying the main body color, we modify the color of the pattern, sleeve, and hem.

We can use the color picker to extract colors from the panel.

Add them to the color palette for repeated use later.

Using the same method, modify the color of the hem and collar fabric.

Now we can see the changes.

Next, we come back to the handmade decorative sewing lines.

We use the sewing line tool to create it.

The thread material is from our folder, a free material I downloaded from our Closet Connect mall.

Right-click it and add it to the workspace.

We use the sewing line tool because I want a cross-stitch effect on the sleeve.

After adding it, zoom in to see the thread added.

You can adjust its attributes in the property editor: length, SPI value, width, diameter, and thickness.

Since this is an OBJ thread, it shows a three-dimensional effect.

Change its color as needed.

Next, we create two sewing lines on this sleeve.

We use the sewing line tool to sew a 1.5mm wide, 200mm long strip.

Apply a new fabric to it.

Change it to black.

We find the sewing position in the 3D window.

Then find the corresponding position on the 2D board.

Here, we create a 1.5mm wide internal strip.

Sew the small piece to it.

Repeat the same operation on the other side.

If the software response is slow, we can turn off the “Display Knitwear” option and then simulate and modify the pattern pieces.

I quickly arranged these two long pattern pieces around the model’s garment.

Then start simulation.

After simulation, we can reduce the particle spacing of these two pieces and increase the render thickness.

This creates a good hanging yarn effect.

Pull out some fabric around the sleeve opening.

Simulate again.

Finally, we can add a texture to the garment.

We provide a preset alpaca wool texture.

Check it in the object window.

We set a hair material here.

Below are specific hair settings.

For hair, you can also check previous videos on hair.

After setting, open the rendering window to see the effect.

Loading takes some time.

Here, I show a pre-rendered image.

Now our basic sweater is finished.

Next, we will modify the knitwear set.

First, this includes a top and pants.

We will start by modifying the pants.

First, turn the pants pattern visible and hide it.

We want to lengthen it.

Find the shape tool in the 3D window toolbar.

Select the bottom circle line of the top.

Shrink it inward.

Since it is shrinking, change the movement distance to a negative value.

Enter -30, click OK.

Then modify the sleeve similarly.

While shrinking, right-click to open the shape line window.

Enter the movement distance.

Look at the back.

Use the move shape line and edit shape line tools to flatten the curve.

You can also adjust the curve in the 2D window.

If the waist is still a bit large, shrink it again.

This makes the work easier.

Click OK multiple times.

After adjusting, use the editor tool to select the line below.

Delete all curve points and convert it to a straight line.

Straighten both sides of the sleeve.

Follow the reference plum red line.

Stretch the sleeve a little longer.

Rearrange.

Use the 3D pen and fashion tool.

Draw a line directly on the 3D window of the dress.

Hold Ctrl to draw curves.

Use the editor tool to adjust the curve.

Right-click on the curve to make it an internal shape.

Go back to the 2D window and remove the joint.

Smooth the curve before cutting.

Do the same on the other side symmetrically.

Pull the right front piece forward slightly.

Right-click effect.

Before simulating, select the neck lines.

Stretch them in the property editor.

Open the stretch bar.

Set a stretch type to prevent over-stretching of the neck.

Move the line down.

Adjust the neck up and down.

If the neck is a bit large, use the texture pen tool to tighten it.

Now the top is basically modified.

Next, we will make a circle of bow ties.

First, use the rectangle tool to draw a rectangular pattern piece of 10×500×10.

Arrange it around the model’s waist.

Adjust its XY position and spacing in the property editor.

I want the piece to start sewing from the model’s left side seam.

Rotate it from back to front, wrapping around to the front center.

Make half first; the other half is a symmetrical copy.

Sew it onto the garment body.

Freeze the main garment pattern piece first.

Sew the bow ties onto the front symmetrically.

Sew one side, then copy symmetrically to the other side.

Sew the front center seam.

Start simulation.

The length is a bit long; we can shorten it from the center outward.

Adjust while observing the effect.

After finishing the front center, merge the bow ties or select the sewing lines and set their strength and thickness to zero to hide obvious seams.

Next, modify the pants.

Show the pants pattern pieces.

I want to taper the knee inward.

Use the circumferential measuring tool to find the knee area.

Right-click on the line and create internal lines.

Since left and right sides are symmetrical, delete the overlapping line and keep one.

Convert it to a straight line.

Select these two internal lines and right-click to add them outside the board.

Shrink the actual points on the side of the screen inward.

When shrinking, the hip width also reduces.

If you want to maintain hip width, use the edit sewing line tool, right-click on the sewing line, and add points at the start.

Then modify.

Shrink the internal line with Ctrl pressed.

Set movement distance to 30.

Start simulation.

Make a segment on the pants.

Hang the internal line first, right-click, and sew it.

Connect the two outer edges.

Split the inner frame in half.

Right-click to extend outside the sheet.

Set extension length to 100mm.

Confirm.

Remember to sew the extended sheet.

The side seam bulges slightly.

Use the round-shape curve tool to pull the edge and make it rounder.

At the waist position, extend outwards.

Use the edition sheet tool.

Select the top line.

Right-click to extend outside the sheet.

Set to 100mm.

Confirm.

Connect the inside of the sheet.

Use the fold-down arrangement tool.

Select the line in the 3D window.

Turn the top sheet downwards.

Turn on simulation to observe.

The back and center are not sewn yet.

Sewing them will shrink the entire sheet upward.

To prevent sliding, fix it.

Use the 3D pen clothing tool.

Draw a line on the pants to fix the position.

Convert the lines into internal shapes.

Done.

Now, using the edit sewing line tool, select the sewn lines.

Set sewing line strength and thickness to zero.

The fold lines have a slight curve; adjust them.

Add 1mm internal lines on both sides of the fold line to subdivide the mesh.

Now the top and pants are modified.

Next, add the underwear garment file from the folder.

Since the knitwear set is slightly transparent, I added a set of underwear.

Change its layer to -1 in the water-based pen and turn on simulation.

Use a gradient blue and purple pattern on the current garment.

Enlarge the texture.

If the gradient position is unsatisfactory, adjust it in cherry blossom arrangement mode.

Click automatic arrangement.

Select all colors.

Align the pants pattern.

Right-click to align.

Move the patterns together to the desired gradient position.

Do the same for the top.

Adjust material positions.

The belt has a waistband pattern.

The pant legs can be set to solid color.

Return to simulation mode.

Copy the material.

This is the belt model.

There is a waist plate, waist section, and ankle split plate.

Set different stitches and colors for each.

First, find these plates and apply fabric.

Use a color picker to absorb colors from the body.

Apply colors to the waist plate.

Delete original textures.

Add adjusted colors to the designated color palette.

Avoid repeating color selection.

Now we have the colors.

Select the big mountain fabric.

Change its material type to knitwear in the property editor.

Choose flat stitch.

Adjust details.

You can reduce edge density and adjust roughness according to the 3D window effect.

Do the same for the belt.

Change its material type to knitwear.

Choose the stitch type.

For the waist, choose a patterned stitch.

For the ankle, check the stitch pattern.

I want the stitch pattern horizontal and parallel to the top and bottom edges.

The default added pattern is vertical.

First, use the adjustment plate tool to change the stitch direction.

Select two plates on the left.

Find custom array on the right.

Select bottom or top line.

Do the same on the right.

After changing stitch direction, use the adjustment plate tool.

Select four plates.

Rotate the stitch direction to the desired orientation.

Change stitch material type to fabric.

Change to patterned stitch.

In the 3D window, you can see the fit pattern parallel to plate edges.

Then adjust density and thickness.

Make yarn thickness smaller.

After adjustment, go to the underwear layer we set earlier.

After simulation, you can change it back.

Colors can also be modified.

Add chosen colors to the palette.

Use the same color for other underwear pattern pieces.

Add them.

Now the entire knitwear set, top and bottom, is modified and stitch types set.

Next, add a five-loop knot belt at the pants waist.

The belt is done.

Add a bow.

First, add the triple-loop chain on the outside.

You can see it here.

Find the bow material in the folder and the clothing document ZPAC.

Choose the second item and add it to the workspace.

It should be in this position.

Find the corresponding position in the 2D board and draw an internal line.

Move the bow closer for easier sewing.

Sew the bow to the belt.

Use the quick arrangement tool for approximate placement.

Pull it out slightly to prevent penetration.

Freeze other pattern pieces during simulation.

Turn on simulation.

Use the bow fabric.

Use belt fabric for the board.

Simulate again.

After finishing, we have a real three-dimensional floral decoration on the bow.

Open another cloud window.

Add it to the clothing document.

First, use curved board tool to draw a small 30×70 board.

This board is half the size of a petal.

Use the internal multidirectional line tool.

Draw the petal shape on this half.

Use adjustment board tool.

Right-click and convert it to a board.

Delete extra left circle.

Lower the armhole slightly.

Align the board.

Open it.

Adjust petal shape again.

Copy it out directly.

Make four copies for a total of five petals.

Use the circular board tool.

Draw a 20-point circular board.

Reduce particle diameter slightly.

Since we have five petal pieces, divide the circle into five equal parts.

Convert ten points into internal free points.

Use the plus point division tool.

Right-click the circle.

Divide into five equal pieces.

Sew the petal again.

Place the round board in the 3D window first.

This is the flower center.

Flip it.

Freeze it.

After sewing all petals, select all petal pieces.

Right-click in 3D window.

Add to side.

Separate the petals first.

Remove hardening.

Using default fabric, petals are soft.

Change to physical attribute.

Choose a harder fabric.

This fabric is hard and sticky.

Adjust petal shape using fixed needles to place them as desired.

After adjusting, select all petals.

Right-click to remove joints.

Set to 5 petal joints.

Set internal line diameter to 2mm.

Cut internal lines and sew.

Adjust petals.

If simulation issues occur, remove cold holes.

Use fixed needle to simulate again.

Copy fabric for edge of petals.

Top of petals same as inside.

Cut front edge and sew in the middle.

You can see the front showing.

Adjust petal size.

Cut edge bottom.

Make sure bottom is not too wide.

Raise edges.

Turn on central line.

Tighten threads.

Since boards face opposite directions now, select all pattern boards.

Turn over their surfaces with right-click.

The outside shows a flat stitch.

Change edges to reverse stitch.

After adjustment, change color of this board.

Add a gradient pattern.

Use white or pure color on edges.

On flower center, use button tool to add a button.

Change button pattern to a round cloth button.

Change button material type to hair.

Set hair parameters.

Use hair to create hair effect on flower center.

Open rendering window to see hair effect.

After finishing this small flower, save it as a clothing file.

Return to the knitwear project file.

Add this flower to the 3D window.

Place it where desired.

Copy a few more flowers.

Use shortcut arrangement tool to quickly arrange all pattern pieces.

Copy and place flowers on shoulders.

Place more as desired.

Now open “Display Knitwear” to check.

We can see the knitwear set modification is complete.

Some details remain, such as at the pant cuffs, pattern edges, sleeve cuffs, and garment hem.

These areas can be further refined with bind-off details.

The method is the same as used earlier for the sweater.

Here is a pre-made render for you to check the effect.

Besides these garments, you can also make knit socks using the knitwear function.

It also works well for plush toys and blankets.

That concludes today’s live broadcast. Thank you all.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to Knitwear Features in Kele 2024.0 This section introduces the new knitwear functionality in Kele 2024.0, focusing on creating garment styles such as sweaters using advanced knit fabric simulation. Key terminology includes knitwear, stitch types, knitting density, wales count, and seam generation. The new version of Kele allows users to create realistic knitwear garments by selecting the fabric and switching the material type to "Knitwear." This replaces previous reliance on fabric texture maps, displacement maps, and replacement maps. The garment surface in the 3D window now visually represents knitted fabric created by needles. Within the property editor under Knitwear, several stitch types are available: - Suspend needle - Plain stitch - Reverse stitch - Single osmanthus stitch - Osmanthus stitch - Ribbing (including 2×2 ribbing) - Half-rib stitch - Honeycomb stitch Users can easily switch between these stitches to achieve different knit textures. Knitting density controls the tightness of the knit: lower values create sparser knitting, higher values tighter knitting. The wales count refers to the number of knitting wales per wale unit and can be set from 1 to 6; each wale can have an individual color. Wales thickness adjusts the thickness of each wale. The software can automatically generate seams, creating outward-extending wales at pattern piece seams to ensure natural connections. Seam bending length controls how far wales extend outward at seams, while seam bending rate controls how much the pattern curls inward at seam and edge positions. The valley line normal map adds bump textures along valley lines, enhancing shadowing effects that add realism to the knit surface. --- ## Customizing Collar, Cuffs, and Hem with Ribbing and Bind-Off Details This section explains how to customize knitwear garment edges such as collars, cuffs, and hems using ribbing stitch types and bind-off techniques to simulate realistic knitting behavior. To apply ribbing, first copy the main garment’s fabric and switch its stitch type to ribbing 2×2. The collar pattern piece can be selected in the 3D window and horizontally scaled down to about 80% to simulate the natural gradual shrinkage and bind-off effect at edges. Before simulation, uncheck the “Display Knitwear” option to speed up processing. The hem and cuffs follow the same process. For detailed bind-off effects, use the Edit Pattern Piece tool to select the outer lines of the collar, hem, and cuffs, set an internal line spacing of 2mm, right-click, and choose Cut and Sew. After modifying, turn “Display Knitwear” back on. Apply a reverse stitch fabric to the newly cut small pattern pieces and adjust their color to match. The surface will then exhibit realistic knitting effects consistent with the bind-off. --- ## Color and Texture Customization of Knitwear Garments This section covers methods to change garment colors and apply textures, including multi-wale color settings and gradient patterns for knitwear. Colors can be customized by setting the number of wales and assigning colors to each wale line. Alternatively, textures can be added below the basic parameters, allowing for gradient or patterned effects.

chunks.content: Apply a reverse stitch fabric to the newly cut small pattern pieces and adjust their color to match. The surface will then exhibit realistic knitting effects consistent with the bind-off. --- ## Color and Texture Customization of Knitwear Garments This section covers methods to change garment colors and apply textures, including multi-wale color settings and gradient patterns for knitwear. Colors can be customized by setting the number of wales and assigning colors to each wale line. Alternatively, textures can be added below the basic parameters, allowing for gradient or patterned effects. For example, a gradient pattern can be dragged onto the texture slot from the material file folder, with the original colors adjusted to white for clarity. The adjustment texture tool can resize the pattern to focus on a single ring. Colors of different garment parts such as the main body, sleeves, hem, and collar can be modified using the color picker, which allows extraction from the panel and addition to a reusable palette. --- ## Adding Decorative Sewing Lines and Thread Effects This section details creating handmade decorative sewing lines with a cross-stitch effect using the sewing line tool and thread materials. Sewing thread materials can be imported from the Closet Connect mall free materials folder and added to the workspace. The sewing line tool allows for precise thread placement on sleeves or garment parts. Thread attributes adjustable in the property editor include length, stitches per inch (SPI), width, diameter, and thickness. OBJ thread types provide 3D effects, and thread colors can be customized. Example: Two sewing lines of 1.5mm width and 200mm length were created on a sleeve with black fabric applied. Positions were aligned between the 3D and 2D windows. If performance slows, turning off "Display Knitwear" during simulation improves responsiveness. Particle spacing and render thickness can be adjusted post-simulation to enhance effects such as hanging yarns. Fabric can be pulled around openings to simulate natural stretching. --- ## Applying Hair Materials and Preset Textures for Realism This section explains how to add preset alpaca wool textures and hair materials to knitwear for realistic surface effects. The alpaca wool texture preset is available in the object window. Hair materials can be applied with adjustable hair-specific parameters to simulate fiber properties. For detailed hair settings, see related tutorials. Rendering the garment after applying hair materials shows improved realism, though loading times may be longer. Pre-rendered images demonstrate the final look. --- ## Modifying Knitwear Sets: Pants and Tops Adjustments This section describes detailed modification techniques for knitwear sets including pants and tops using shape tools, editing lines, and sewing adjustments. For pants: - Use the shape tool to shrink the bottom circle line inward by entering a negative movement value (e.g., -30). - Flatten curves using move and edit shape line tools. - Adjust waist width by shrinking pattern pieces; maintain hip width by adding points to sewing lines. - Create internal lines at the knee area to taper inward using circumferential measuring.

chunks.content: --- ## Modifying Knitwear Sets: Pants and Tops Adjustments This section describes detailed modification techniques for knitwear sets including pants and tops using shape tools, editing lines, and sewing adjustments. For pants: - Use the shape tool to shrink the bottom circle line inward by entering a negative movement value (e.g., -30). - Flatten curves using move and edit shape line tools. - Adjust waist width by shrinking pattern pieces; maintain hip width by adding points to sewing lines. - Create internal lines at the knee area to taper inward using circumferential measuring. - Extend internal lines outside the pattern board by 100mm and sew them. - Round edges and extend waist areas outward for better fit. - Use fold-down arrangement tools to position sheets during simulation. - Fix pattern pieces with 3D pen clothing tools to prevent sliding. - Set sewing line strength and thickness to zero to hide seams. - Add 1mm internal lines beside fold lines to subdivide mesh for smoother curves. For tops: - Stretch necklines carefully using the property editor's stretch bar with stretch types to avoid over-stretching. - Use the texture pen tool to tighten loose neck areas. - Draw internal shapes and smooth curves with 3D pen and editor tools. - Symmetrically modify sleeves and front pieces. --- ## Creating and Sewing Bow Tie Decorations This section outlines the process of creating a circle of bow ties for the garment waist, including pattern creation, positioning, sewing, and simulation. - Draw a rectangular pattern piece (10×500×10). - Arrange the piece around the model’s waist, adjusting XY position and spacing. - Start sewing from the model's left side seam. - Rotate the piece around the waist, creating half and copying it symmetrically for the other half. - Sew bow ties onto the garment body, freezing main garment pieces to avoid interference. - Adjust bow tie length symmetrically from the center after simulation. - Merge bow ties or set sewing line strength and thickness to zero to hide seams. --- ## Tapering and Adjusting Pants with Internal Lines and Sewing This section describes tapering pants at the knee and other fit adjustments using internal lines and sewing techniques. - Use the circumferential measuring tool to locate the knee. - Create internal lines, convert to straight lines, delete duplicates to maintain symmetry. - Add external lines from internal lines by extending 100mm. - Shrink pattern points inward while maintaining hip width via editing sewing lines. - Sew new lines and simulate. - Round bulging side seams using round-shape curve tools. - Extend waist area outward using editing sheet tools. - Fold down sheets and fix positions to prevent sliding. - Subdivide meshes with internal lines beside folds for better deformation. --- ## Adding Underwear Layer and Gradient Textures This section covers adding an underwear garment layer beneath the knitwear for opacity and color enhancement. - Import underwear garment file and set its layer to -1. - Turn on simulation and apply gradient blue-purple patterns.

markdown_content: ## Introduction to Knitwear Features in Kele 2024.0 This section introduces the new knitwear functionality in Kele 2024.0, focusing on creating garment styles such as sweaters using advanced knit fabric simulation. Key terminology includes knitwear, stitch types, knitting density, wales count, and seam generation. The new version of Kele allows users to create realistic knitwear garments by selecting the fabric and switching the material type to "Knitwear." This replaces previous reliance on fabric texture maps, displacement maps, and replacement maps. The garment surface in the 3D window now visually represents knitted fabric created by needles. Within the property editor under Knitwear, several stitch types are available: - Suspend needle - Plain stitch - Reverse stitch - Single osmanthus stitch - Osmanthus stitch - Ribbing (including 2×2 ribbing) - Half-rib stitch - Honeycomb stitch Users can easily switch between these stitches to achieve different knit textures. Knitting density controls the tightness of the knit: lower values create sparser knitting, higher values tighter knitting. The wales count refers to the number of knitting wales per wale unit and can be set from 1 to 6; each wale can have an individual color. Wales thickness adjusts the thickness of each wale. The software can automatically generate seams, creating outward-extending wales at pattern piece seams to ensure natural connections. Seam bending length controls how far wales extend outward at seams, while seam bending rate controls how much the pattern curls inward at seam and edge positions. The valley line normal map adds bump textures along valley lines, enhancing shadowing effects that add realism to the knit surface. --- ## Customizing Collar, Cuffs, and Hem with Ribbing and Bind-Off Details This section explains how to customize knitwear garment edges such as collars, cuffs, and hems using ribbing stitch types and bind-off techniques to simulate realistic knitting behavior. To apply ribbing, first copy the main garment’s fabric and switch its stitch type to ribbing 2×2. The collar pattern piece can be selected in the 3D window and horizontally scaled down to about 80% to simulate the natural gradual shrinkage and bind-off effect at edges. Before simulation, uncheck the “Display Knitwear” option to speed up processing. The hem and cuffs follow the same process. For detailed bind-off effects, use the Edit Pattern Piece tool to select the outer lines of the collar, hem, and cuffs, set an internal line spacing of 2mm, right-click, and choose Cut and Sew. After modifying, turn “Display Knitwear” back on. Apply a reverse stitch fabric to the newly cut small pattern pieces and adjust their color to match. The surface will then exhibit realistic knitting effects consistent with the bind-off. --- ## Color and Texture Customization of Knitwear Garments This section covers methods to change garment colors and apply textures, including multi-wale color settings and gradient patterns for knitwear. Colors can be customized by setting the number of wales and assigning colors to each wale line. Alternatively, textures can be added below the basic parameters, allowing for gradient or patterned effects. For example, a gradient pattern can be dragged onto the texture slot from the material file folder, with the original colors adjusted to white for clarity. The adjustment texture tool can resize the pattern to focus on a single ring. Colors of different garment parts such as the main body, sleeves, hem, and collar can be modified using the color picker, which allows extraction from the panel and addition to a reusable palette. --- ## Adding Decorative Sewing Lines and Thread Effects This section details creating handmade decorative sewing lines with a cross-stitch effect using the sewing line tool and thread materials. Sewing thread materials can be imported from the Closet Connect mall free materials folder and added to the workspace. The sewing line tool allows for precise thread placement on sleeves or garment parts. Thread attributes adjustable in the property editor include length, stitches per inch (SPI), width, diameter, and thickness. OBJ thread types provide 3D effects, and thread colors can be customized. Example: Two sewing lines of 1.5mm width and 200mm length were created on a sleeve with black fabric applied. Positions were aligned between the 3D and 2D windows. If performance slows, turning off "Display Knitwear" during simulation improves responsiveness. Particle spacing and render thickness can be adjusted post-simulation to enhance effects such as hanging yarns. Fabric can be pulled around openings to simulate natural stretching. --- ## Applying Hair Materials and Preset Textures for Realism This section explains how to add preset alpaca wool textures and hair materials to knitwear for realistic surface effects. The alpaca wool texture preset is available in the object window. Hair materials can be applied with adjustable hair-specific parameters to simulate fiber properties. For detailed hair settings, see related tutorials. Rendering the garment after applying hair materials shows improved realism, though loading times may be longer. Pre-rendered images demonstrate the final look. --- ## Modifying Knitwear Sets: Pants and Tops Adjustments This section describes detailed modification techniques for knitwear sets including pants and tops using shape tools, editing lines, and sewing adjustments. For pants: - Use the shape tool to shrink the bottom circle line inward by entering a negative movement value (e.g., -30). - Flatten curves using move and edit shape line tools. - Adjust waist width by shrinking pattern pieces; maintain hip width by adding points to sewing lines. - Create internal lines at the knee area to taper inward using circumferential measuring. - Extend internal lines outside the pattern board by 100mm and sew them. - Round edges and extend waist areas outward for better fit. - Use fold-down arrangement tools to position sheets during simulation. - Fix pattern pieces with 3D pen clothing tools to prevent sliding. - Set sewing line strength and thickness to zero to hide seams. - Add 1mm internal lines beside fold lines to subdivide mesh for smoother curves. For tops: - Stretch necklines carefully using the property editor's stretch bar with stretch types to avoid over-stretching. - Use the texture pen tool to tighten loose neck areas. - Draw internal shapes and smooth curves with 3D pen and editor tools. - Symmetrically modify sleeves and front pieces. --- ## Creating and Sewing Bow Tie Decorations This section outlines the process of creating a circle of bow ties for the garment waist, including pattern creation, positioning, sewing, and simulation. - Draw a rectangular pattern piece (10×500×10). - Arrange the piece around the model’s waist, adjusting XY position and spacing. - Start sewing from the model's left side seam. - Rotate the piece around the waist, creating half and copying it symmetrically for the other half. - Sew bow ties onto the garment body, freezing main garment pieces to avoid interference. - Adjust bow tie length symmetrically from the center after simulation. - Merge bow ties or set sewing line strength and thickness to zero to hide seams. --- ## Tapering and Adjusting Pants with Internal Lines and Sewing This section describes tapering pants at the knee and other fit adjustments using internal lines and sewing techniques. - Use the circumferential measuring tool to locate the knee. - Create internal lines, convert to straight lines, delete duplicates to maintain symmetry. - Add external lines from internal lines by extending 100mm. - Shrink pattern points inward while maintaining hip width via editing sewing lines. - Sew new lines and simulate. - Round bulging side seams using round-shape curve tools. - Extend waist area outward using editing sheet tools. - Fold down sheets and fix positions to prevent sliding. - Subdivide meshes with internal lines beside folds for better deformation. --- ## Adding Underwear Layer and Gradient Textures This section covers adding an underwear garment layer beneath the knitwear for opacity and color enhancement. - Import underwear garment file and set its layer to -1. - Turn on simulation and apply gradient blue-purple patterns. - Use cherry blossom arrangement mode to adjust gradient positioning. - Align pants and tops pattern pieces for consistent gradient effect. - Set solid colors for pant legs and adjust belt waistband separately. - Copy materials and apply appropriate stitch types and colors for belt components. - Reduce edge density and adjust roughness for better appearance. --- ## Customizing Stitch Direction and Pattern on Knitwear Components This section explains how to adjust stitch direction and pattern alignment on complex garment plates such as belts and waistbands. - Select plates and apply knitwear material type with flat stitch. - Use adjustment plate tool to customize stitch direction by selecting top or bottom lines. - Rotate stitch patterns to be horizontal and parallel to top and bottom edges. - Change stitch material type to patterned stitch. - Adjust density, thickness, and yarn thickness for desired texture. - Apply consistent colors by sampling from body fabrics and adding to palettes. --- ## Adding Three-Dimensional Floral Decorations This section details the creation of a 3D floral decoration consisting of petals and center flower components, including pattern drawing, sewing, fabric selection, and simulation. - Draw a 30×70 curved board representing half a petal. - Use internal multidirectional line tools to define petal shape. - Duplicate petals to create a full five-petal flower. - Draw a circular 20-point board divided into five equal parts for flower center. - Sew petals and flower center, positioning in 3D window. - Adjust fabric physical attributes for petal hardness and stickiness. - Use fixed needles to shape petals as desired. - Remove joints and add internal lines for sewing with 2mm diameter. - Cut and sew petal edges, tightening threads and raising edges for realism. - Flip petals to correct outside orientation. - Apply flat stitch on petal faces and reverse stitch on edges
